body.text: The early signs of a nation’s decline appear when it fails to provide essential services and security to its people. Once failure takes hold across every front, it leads irreversibly to the collapse of governments—a pattern that has been playing out across the world today. Veteran diplomat Ambassador Rajiv Dogra’s book How Nations Fail gives a vivid account of the factors that make a nation great, or why, having become great, it falters.

History has repeatedly witnessed the rise and fall of civilisations, empires and nations. Dogra asserts that failures are inevitable: only their timing and form vary. The longevity and well-being of a nation depend on the quality of its leadership. The institutions that leaders create and sustain help enforce rights and duties which, in turn, promote economic development, stability and inclusivity. Prosperity may induce ideas for conquest, and it is here that the seeds of decline are sown.

Dogra reasons that expansion carries within itself the seeds of exhaustion that eventually bring empires down. Of the 22 civilisations of the world, Dogra notes, only the Indian and Chinese civilisations have survived, while the rest have either perished or been transformed beyond recognition. Restraint prolongs a ruler’s reign—a lesson borne out by empire-builders from Alexander and Cyrus to Julius Caesar, Ashoka, and the Chola kings. Across time, empires, the Greeks, the Romans, the Mughals and the British all made the same mistake—abandoning the principles that made them great in the first place.

The cyclical nature of war is aptly captured by Charles Tilly’s dictum that “war made the state, and the state made war”. Dogra emphasises that this holds true for all ages, as wars bring about death, destruction and financial ruin. The post-Second World War period has been marked by intense conflict in which 22 million people are said to have died in 150 wars.

In this era of great power competition, the seeds of mutually assured destruction are already embedded. Attempts at grabbing others’ lands—think Ukraine, Gaza, Greenland, and Taiwan, for instance—may plunge the world into forever wars in which smaller players may be drawn to act in concert. One would do well to recall the Greek historian Thucydides’ poignant conclusion from the PeloponnesianWar that “the strong do what they will, and the weak suffer what they must”. But today the weak are also fighting back to uphold their sense of national dignity. The stand-off between Ukraine and Iran, on the one side, and the superpowers on the other, aided by affordable drone technology, is prolonging wars with global ramifications.
How Nations Fail and the Unmaking of America’s World

While dishonesty among politicians is nothing new, Dogra finds the erosion of character in leaders today especially distressing. Their tactics of deception and misinformation, he argues, will hasten the decay of democracy, inflicting lasting harm to ordinary people. Today, Dogra says, the limits of US hegemony can be attributed to its leadership crisis, both domestic and international. Managing competition in the age of interdependence may be the litmus test of its global leadership. Increasingly, China’s rise is seen as evidence of the US’ decline. Europe, too, suffers from similar leadership lapses, a kind of “Peter Principle” that casts doubts on its solidity. Brexit, the Ukraine war, a fractious NATO, and the immigration crisis only deepen scepticism about the patchwork quilt that is Europe. About 70 per cent of the world population is said to live under some form of authoritarianism and Dogra warns that AI will only exacerbate this existential risk to humanity.

Dogra is uncomfortable with the extraordinary personality cult that envelops Indian political leaders, noting that it pushes them towards impulsive decisions such as demonetisation, the inept implementation of GST, the hasty farm laws, and the mishandling of the COVID-19 lockdown, to name but a few. The growing wealth inequality, with the top 1 per cent holding 40.1 per cent in 2022–23, according to the World Inequality Report 2024, is disturbing. The report finds that the billionaire Raj is now more unequal than the British Raj.

Dogra argues that India’s foreign policy is detached from domestic reality, often straying from the civilisational entity that India once was. Despite these stumbles, he remains confident about India’s future, with its youth leading the way. For a deeper understanding of this theme, readers may also wish to read Dogra’s other books: India’s World: How Prime Ministers Shaped Foreign Policy;Wartime:The World in Danger; Autocrats: Charisma, Power and Their Lives.

The optimist in Dogra sees in every fall a hint of a fresh spring and the beginning of a new rise. If the world order is to survive, he argues, it will have to function as a global democracy that balances the priorities of the North with the aspirations of the South. He also asserts that this new order requires framing global rules on which India should take the lead. India’s ancient wisdom, flowing from Kautilya’s Arthashastra, holds that “in the happiness of his subjects lies the king’s happiness”. It finds resonance in the historian Arnold J. Toynbee’s thought that “the chapter of humanity which had a Western beginning will have to have an Indian ending, if it is not to end in self-destruction of the human race”.
Dammu Ravi is a retired Indian Foreign Service Officer.
